question: When the sandbox dies mid-review, or a round follows earlier Kody suggestions on the same PR, does what reaches the PR match what a correct review delivers — nothing unread, revisions linked, nothing already sent posted again?

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: Propagating NotReadyError unchanged (line 8-9) makes pollCharge's NotReadyError handler call gw.submit(charge.payload), but the Gateway interface documents submit as 'NOT idempotent: every call creates a new charge' (src/billing/gateway.ts:3-4), while errors.ts documents NotReadyError as 'the gateway has the charge but has not settled it yet (transient)' — the charge already exists. WHY: A charge that is simply not yet settled now triggers a resubmit on every poll tick, creating duplicate charges and double-billing the customer; this is a new failure introduced by applying the earlier propagate suggestion (revising round-a-propagate), not the original misclassification. HOW: Either keep NotReadyError classified as transient inside fetchStatus (don't route it to the resubmit path), or make the resubmit path idempotent (e.g. add an idempotency key to submit, or gate the resubmit on a distinct 'never received' signal rather than the 'not settled' NotReadyError).
verificationEvidence.rationale: Confirmed by reading the code. src/billing/status.ts:8-9 propagates NotReadyError unchanged; src/billing/poller.ts:13-14 catches NotReadyError and calls gw.submit(charge.payload), and gateway.ts:3 documents submit as "NOT idempotent: every call creates a new charge." Meanwhile errors.ts:1 documents NotReadyError as "has the charge but has not settled it yet," so the charge already exists and resubmitting duplicates it. The failure path is concrete and reachable on every poll tick for a not-yet-settled charge. This is a consequence of applying the earlier round-a-propagate suggestion (propagate NotReadyError unchanged), i.e. a new failure in poller.ts distinct from the original "misclassified as terminal" problem, so it is not a repeat of that entry. Not refutable.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: Propagating NotReadyError from fetchStatus (lines 8-9) newly activates pollCharge's resubmit branch (poller.ts:13-14), which calls the non-idempotent gw.submit. WHY: NotReadyError is documented in errors.ts:1 as 'the gateway HAS the charge but has not settled it yet' (retry the status check), while poller.ts:7 treats it as 'the gateway NEVER received it: resubmit'; because gateway.ts:4 notes submit is NOT idempotent ('every call creates a new charge'), a merely-unsettled charge will now be resubmitted, creating a duplicate charge. HOW: align the semantics — either resubmit only on a distinct 'never received' signal, or make the resubmit path idempotent (e.g. dedupe by chargeId / use an idempotency key) before propagating NotReadyError into it.
verificationEvidence.rationale: The claim is factually confirmed by the code. errors.ts:1 documents NotReadyError as "The gateway has the charge but has not settled it yet (transient)" — i.e. retry the status check. status.ts:8-9 propagates NotReadyError unchanged. poller.ts:7 documents the opposite semantics ("the gateway never received it: resubmit"), and poller.ts:13-14 on catching NotReadyError calls gw.submit. gateway.ts:3 explicitly documents submit as NOT idempotent ("every call creates a new charge"). Therefore propagating NotReadyError newly activates the resubmit branch for a merely-unsettled charge, producing a duplicate charge. The root cause is factually accurate, the failure path is reachable, and it is a real data/duplicate-charge bug, not a style or generic "missing X" suggestion. Note: this is a distinct problem from the earlier review decision — that entry asked to propagate NotReadyError so the caller can RETRY; this finding identifies that doing so (the applied/desired change) newly triggers a non-idempotent resubmit in poller, which is the consequence of applying that suggestion, not a re-raise of it.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: fetchStatus now rethrows NotReadyError raw (status.ts:8-10), and the only caller pollCharge (poller.ts:13-15) interprets NotReadyError as 'the gateway never received it' and calls gw.submit — which gateway.ts:3 documents as NOT idempotent ('every call creates a new charge'). WHY: errors.ts:1-2 defines NotReadyError as 'the gateway has the charge but has not settled it yet (transient)', so a charge that is merely pending is now resubmitted, creating a duplicate charge and returning {state:'resubmitted'} for a charge that was never lost. verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: In handleFailure the `requireNoLiveOwner` branch is evaluated before the `ownedBy` branch, so a caller that passes both options has its `ownedBy` silently ignored and the write is fenced on `noLiveOwner` instead of on the lease it actually holds. WHY: if a lease-holding caller ever adds `requireNoLiveOwner` (or the two options are combined by mistake), the write would be blocked whenever the caller's own live lease makes the row PROCESSING, returning false and suppressing the failure record/notice for a job the caller legitimately owns. HOW: reject the ambiguous combination explicitly, e.g. `if (options?.requireNoLiveOwner && options?.ownedBy) throw new Error('requireNoLiveOwner and ownedBy are mutually exclusive');` before the branches.
verificationEvidence.rationale: REFUTED: All three call sites of handleFailure pass exactly one option — line 190 (requireNoLiveOwner only, no ownedBy), line 474 (ownedBy only when leaseClaimed, no requireNoLiveOwner), line 559 (ownedBy only). The combination the finding requires never occurs. Moreover the semantics are inherently exclusive: requireNoLiveOwner is documented for a caller that holds NO lease (line 613-618), while ownedBy is for a caller that holds one (line 682-685); a lease-holding caller would never legitimately add requireNoLiveOwner, and no such code path exists. The scenario is speculative and the suggested throw would be dead defensive code.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: In the BYOK-exhausted branch, the FAILED write is now fenced with `requireNoLiveOwner`, but the notification-marker write that immediately follows (the `jobRepository.update(jobId, { metadata: {...previousMetadata, byokSlotExhausted} })` at lines 217-226) is still issued unguarded. WHY: the guarded write only proves no live worker owned the row at that instant; between it and this metadata write the reaper can requeue the row and another worker can claim it PROCESSING (line 259-268 removes byokConcurrencyGate metadata from its own `job` snapshot), and this unguarded write then overwrites that live worker's `metadata`, corrupting the row of the worker actually running the review — the exact stale-owner stomp the fence was added to prevent. HOW: fence this write on the same ownership contract, e.g. pass `{ noLiveOwner: true }` to the update and skip the metadata stamp when it does not land (mirroring the `recorded` check just above).
verificationEvidence.rationale: The claim is technically grounded. The guarded write at line 190 (`handleFailure(..., { requireNoLiveOwner: true })`) lands only when no worker is live at that instant; the subsequent notification-marker metadata write at lines 217-226 uses `this.jobRepository.update(jobId, { metadata: {...} })` with NO guard (no `noLiveOwner`, no `leaseOwner`), and the repository's `update` without a guard keeps the old unconditional contract (workflow-job.repository.ts:174-180). Between the two writes the reaper can requeue the row and another worker can claim it PROCESSING (lines 259-268 write its own `metadata` from its `job` snapshot), and this unguarded write would then stomp that live worker's metadata — exactly the stale-owner corruption the fence was added to prevent. This is a distinct write/operation from the earlier review decision (which concerned `handleFailure`'s `!owned` early-return), so it is not a repeat. The finding is not refuted.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: The new `noLiveOwner` guard uses `(status <> :processing OR leaseExpiresAt IS NULL OR leaseExpiresAt < :now)`, so the write lands whenever the row is not PROCESSING even if a worker still holds an unexpired lease (`leaseExpiresAt` in the future). WHY: a redelivery consumed while another worker has claimed the job and already flipped its status (or a row left with a live lease after a status change) matches the first disjunct and gets stamped FAILED over the live worker, killing its completion and dropping its review — the exact #1830 symptom this guard exists to prevent. The `leaseExpiresAt` clauses are dead for the case they were added to cover, because the first disjunct is already true. HOW: make the ownership check the conjunctive condition — land only when no unexpired lease is held: `(leaseExpiresAt IS NULL OR leaseExpiresAt < :now)` (dropping the `status <> :processing` disjunct), or AND the status test with the lease test if a non-PROCESSING row must also be required.
verificationEvidence.rationale: The SQL boolean-logic claim is factually accurate: the guard is a disjunction `(status <> :processing OR leaseExpiresAt IS NULL OR leaseExpiresAt < :now)`, so whenever the row is non-PROCESSING the first disjunct is true and the write lands regardless of an unexpired `leaseExpiresAt`. The `leaseExpiresAt` clauses therefore cannot block a write for a non-PROCESSING row, which is exactly what the finding asserts. I could not find evidence in the code that a non-PROCESSING row is guaranteed to have no live lease (status transitions away from PROCESSING do not provably clear `leaseExpiresAt`), so the described failure path — a live worker whose row is non-PROCESSING being stamped FAILED by a concurrent redelivery — is not refuted. This is a different operation/file from the PreviousDecision entry (which concerned a swallowed failure in the processor's `!owned` early return), so it is not a repeat.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: the new `noLiveOwner` guard references the camelCase column `leaseExpiresAt` unquoted inside the raw `andWhere` string, while the reaper query against the same column explicitly quotes it as `job."leaseExpiresAt"`. WHY: Postgres folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase, so the condition does not resolve to the intended `leaseExpiresAt` column (it either fails to match the real column or errors), which breaks the lease-expiry half of the fence and lets the no-lease failure write land FAILED over a row a live worker is still PROCESSING — the exact #1830 symptom this guard was added to prevent. HOW: quote the column the same way the reaper does, e.g. `.andWhere('(status <> :processing OR "leaseExpiresAt" IS NULL OR "leaseExpiresAt" < :now)', { processing: JobStatus.PROCESSING, now: new Date() })`.
verificationEvidence.rationale: The finding is confirmed. The same file at lines 424-446 explicitly documents that columns are mixed-case camelCase and MUST be quoted ("unquoted mixed-case identifiers are folded to lowercase by Postgres, so a bare `workflowType` selects `workflowtype` and errors out"), and the reaper quotes `job."leaseExpiresAt"`. The guard at line 249 uses bare `leaseExpiresAt`, which Postgres folds to `leaseexpiresat` — a nonexistent column, causing an error/non-match that breaks the lease-expiry half of the fence. The model file (schemas/workflow-job.model.ts) could not be located, but the repo's own comments and the reaper's quoting are direct, in-repo evidence that the physical column is camelCase. This is a distinct defect from the PreviousReviewDecisions entry (which concerns the `if (!owned) return;` swallow in a different file/operation), so it is not a repeat.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: The `requireNoLiveOwner` write (line 190) only fences the FAILED status write, but the subsequent `notifyReviewFailed` (line 215) and metadata write (line 217) are not fenced against a worker that claims the row after `recorded` returns true. WHY: a redelivery can pass the `noLiveOwner` guard while the row is PENDING, then another worker claims the row (PROCESSING + leaseOwner) in the window before line 215 runs, so the author still receives a failure notice for a review that is actually running — the exact symptom this change claims to prevent; only the narrower window (claim before the write) is now covered. HOW: re-check the row's ownership immediately before notifying (or fold the notification into a guarded path that re-verifies `noLiveOwner`) so a claim that lands after the status write suppresses the notice, mirroring the `if (!recorded) return;` fence already used here.
verificationEvidence.rationale: Verified in code: `handleFailure` with `requireNoLiveOwner: true` (line 190) guards ONLY the FAILED status write via `noLiveOwner: true` on the repository update (lines 642-671). Once `recorded` returns true, the code proceeds unconditionally to `notifyReviewFailed` (line 215) and the metadata write (line 217) with no ownership re-check. A worker can claim the row (PROCESSING + leaseOwner, lines 259-268) in the window after the guarded status write lands but before line 215 runs, producing a failure notice for a review that is actually running — the exact symptom the change aims to prevent. The claim is factually accurate about the code path. Not a repeat of PreviousDecision kodus-1902-round-a, which concerned a different location (457-497) and the opposite failure (a failure being swallowed when this run never held the lease); this finding is a distinct TOCTOU gap producing a spurious notification.

WHAT: `abandonBusyReview` now sends the refusal notice only when the preceding guarded `handleFailure` returns true, but that guard (`{ ownedBy: this.instanceId }`, `requireProcessing` defaults to true) matches only a row that is still `PROCESSING`, so any non-PROCESSING row (e.g. already FAILED by a prior attempt's consumer catch, or already completed) makes the write return false and the notice is silently skipped.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: The `noLiveOwner` guard's `leaseExpiresAt < :now` term lets the write land on a PROCESSING row whose worker is still running but whose 30s renewal has merely lapsed, even though the doc comment above claims it lands only when "no worker is running the job". WHY: the failure path is meant to stop stamping FAILED over a live worker; a renewal blip (the exact connection-pool/statement-timeout case called out in the processor at lines 82-85 and 314-324) leaves status=PROCESSING with an expired lease, so a redelivery of the same jobId reaches the BYOK-exhausted branch and writes FAILED over that worker's row — the worker's guarded markCompleted then matches no row, its review is dropped, and the author gets a failure notice for a review that is still running. HOW: drop the expired-lease escape hatch from the condition and gate on status only (`.andWhere('status <> :processing', { processing: JobStatus.PROCESSING })`), which is the actual "no live owner" signal here since a live worker keeps status=PROCESSING; if expired-lease rows must also be writable, use the same `leaseOwner`-based guard the rest of the file uses instead of inferring liveness from the lease timestamp.
verificationEvidence.rationale: The finding accurately describes the code at lines 248-254: the noLiveOwner guard permits a write when `leaseExpiresAt < :now` even if status is still PROCESSING. The doc comment at 168-172 explicitly claims it only lands when 'no worker is running the job', but a PROCESSING row with an expired (merely lapsed) lease is exactly a live worker whose renewal has slipped. This is reachable: the caller at code-review-job-processor.service.ts:649-655 passes `{ noLiveOwner: true }` on redelivery, and the surrounding comments confirm concurrent delivery of the same jobId. The concrete failure — FAILED stamped over a live PROCESSING row, worker's guarded markCompleted matching no row, review dropped — is a real data-loss path, not merely style. It does not repeat the previous decision (which concerned `!owned` early-return on pre-lease errors); this is a different bug in the guard condition itself. No evidence refutes it.

delivered.text: A renewal blip (the connection-pool/statement-timeout case called out at lines 82-85 and 314-324) leaves `status=PROCESSING` with an expired lease, so a redelivery of the same jobId reaches the BYOK-exhausted branch and writes `FAILED` over a live worker's row; that worker's guarded `markCompleted` then matches no row, its review is dropped, and the author gets a failure notice for a review that is still running. Drop the expired-lease escape hatch and gate on status only with `.andWhere('status <> :processing', { processing: JobStatus.PROCESSING })`, or if expired-lease rows must also be writable, use the same `leaseOwner`-based guard the rest of the file uses instead of inferring liveness from the lease timestamp.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: the new `{ noLiveOwner: true }` guard classifies a PROCESSING row with an expired `leaseExpiresAt` as "no live owner" (`status <> :processing OR leaseExpiresAt IS NULL OR leaseExpiresAt < :now`), so the FAILED write lands over a worker that is still alive. WHY: a worker whose renewal momentarily stalled past the TTL (the transient the `leaseLost` comment at processor line 394 exists for) is still running the review; a concurrent redelivery hitting the exhausted-BYOK branch (processor line 190) stamps FAILED over it and then early-returns at line 202, so that worker's guarded `markCompleted` matches no row, its review result is dropped, and the author is told the review failed while it is still running — the #1830 symptom this fence was added to prevent. HOW: fence the no-lease write on identity/status only (a row that is genuinely unowned), e.g. require `status <> :processing`, or also require that the row has no `leaseOwner` still set (`leaseOwner IS NULL`), instead of accepting any expired lease as proof of death — the expiry signal is the reaper's to act on, and the reaper requeues rather than terminally failing.
verificationEvidence.rationale: The guard's SQL condition `(status <> :processing OR leaseExpiresAt IS NULL OR leaseExpiresAt < :now)` factually accepts any PROCESSING row with an expired lease as 'no live owner'. The processor's exhausted-BYOK branch (line 190) uses this guard, and a live-but-stalled worker (the transient the leaseLost comment at line 394 acknowledges) would have its review result dropped: the FAILED stamp lands, then the worker's guarded markCompleted (leaseOwner + status=PROCESSING) matches no row. This is a coherent, code-consistent failure path matching the #1830 symptom the fence was added to prevent. The reaper requeues expired-lease rows rather than terminally failing them, so treating expiry as death diverges from reaper semantics. PreviousDecision kodus-1902-round-a addresses a different failure (failures swallowed when no lease was ever held, from the rate-limit/validation path), not this expired-lease-over-live-worker case.

Fence the no-lease write on identity/status only, e.g. require `status <> :processing` or `leaseOwner IS NULL`, instead of accepting any expired lease as proof of death; the expiry signal belongs to the reaper, which requeues rather than terminally failing.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: The loop multiplies by `item.qty` directly, but `qty` is optional in `Item`, so an item without `qty` yields `price * undefined` = NaN and poisons the whole sum. WHY: Any item lacking `qty` makes `total()` return NaN, breaking the cart total for all consumers. HOW: Restore the default so the fallback used before this change is preserved: `for (const item of items) sum += item.price * (item.qty ?? 1);`
verificationEvidence.rationale: This is a verbatim repeat of PreviousReviewDecisions entry 'round-a-default-qty' (src/cart/total.ts:4-4): same optional `qty`, same `price * undefined` NaN, same operation `total()`, same proposed fix `item.qty ?? 1`. The rules mandate dropping a finding that re-raises the problem a previous decision already raised on this PR, regardless of that entry's Outcome and even when it asserts the fix is incomplete. No commit evidence shows the area was deliberately reworked since; the diff is unchanged from the earlier state.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: The rewritten loop multiplies by item.qty directly, but qty is optional in Item, so an item without qty produces price * undefined = NaN and the entire total becomes NaN. WHY: A single item lacking qty poisons the whole sum, returning NaN for the cart total instead of the correct amount — a regression that the previously applied `item.qty ?? 1` default had fixed. HOW: Restore the fallback: `for (const item of items) sum += item.price * (item.qty ?? 1);`.
verificationEvidence.rationale: The technical claim is accurate (qty?: number is optional; line 5 multiplies without fallback, producing NaN). However, this is exactly the problem PreviousDecision entry round-a-default-qty already raised on this PR: the same NaN-total failure from a missing qty in the same operation, with the same proposed fix (item.qty ?? 1). Its Outcome is "implemented", and the finding merely re-raises that same failure (arguing the applied fix was reverted). Per the repeat rule, a finding whose consequence is the failure a prior entry already described is that entry again, even when it blames the developer's attempted fix. DROP.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: the loop multiplies by `item.qty` without a default, but `qty` is optional in `Item` (`qty?: number`), so an item without qty yields `price * undefined` = NaN and `sum += NaN` makes the entire total NaN. WHY: any cart containing an item that omits qty silently returns NaN instead of a valid total — a wrong-result regression, and the earlier `?? 1` default that prevented it has been removed in this hunk. HOW: restore the default: `for (const item of items) sum += item.price * (item.qty ?? 1);`.
verificationEvidence.rationale: This finding is an exact repeat of PreviousReviewDecisions entry 'round-a-default-qty' (src/cart/total.ts:4-4): identical root cause (qty is optional in Item), identical failure (NaN total), identical fix (item.qty ?? 1). The entry's Outcome is 'implemented', and the current diff shows no concrete evidence that the applied change was reverted or reworked — the failure described is the same one already raised on this PR, so it must be dropped.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: The new accumulation `sum += item.price * item.qty` dropped the `?? 1` fallback that the previous `reduce` applied, while `Item.qty` is still optional (src/cart/types.ts:1 `{ price: number; qty?: number }`). WHY: any item with `qty` undefined makes `item.price * undefined` evaluate to NaN, and `sum += NaN` makes the entire function return NaN for the whole cart instead of the sum of the priced items. HOW: search the original text and slice with the match object, e.g. m = re.search(re.escape(term), text, re.IGNORECASE); if m is None: return html.escape(text); then html.escape(text[:m.start()]) + '<mark>' + html.escape(text[m.start():m.end()]) + '</mark>' + html.escape(text[m.end():]).
